## Recap - Open Set

We have defined what is an open set which is a member of $\tau$,

::: block
### Definition 2.2

Let $(X,\tau)$ be any topological space. Then the members of $\tau$ are said to be **open sets**.
:::

::: block
### Proposition 2.3

If $(X,\tau)$ be any topological space, then:

\
(i) $X$ and $\emptyset$ are open sets,

\(ii\) The union of any collection of sets in $\tau$ is an open set, and

\(iii\) The intersection of any finite collection of sets in $\tau$ is an open set.
:::

But back then in high school, we have open interval and closed interval as well, so how about set?

## Closed Set

::: block
### Definition 4.1

Let $(X,\tau)$ be a topological space. A subset $S$ of $X$ is said to be a **closed set** in $(X,\tau)$ if its **complement** in $X$, namely $X\setminus S$, **is open** in $(X,\tau)$.
:::

::: block
### Proposition 4.2

If $(X,\tau)$ is any topological space, then

\(i\) $\emptyset$ and $X$ are closed set,

\(ii\) the intersection of any (finite or infinite) number of closed sets is a closed set, and

\(iii\) the union of any finite number of closed sets is a closed set.
:::

## Closed Set (cont.)

\vspace{2mm}

Remember that a set, $S$, is closed if $X\setminus S$ is open.

- You can see that $\emptyset = X\setminus X$ is an open set, so $X$ is closed.

- and $X=X\setminus \emptyset$ is an open set, so $\emptyset$ is closed.

- let say $C$ is a closed set, so $(X\setminus C)$ is an open set. Then take the union of this open set, $\bigcup (X\setminus C) = X\setminus \bigcap C$ is an open set (from the definition of open set), so $\bigcap C$ is closed.

- and you can use the same method to prove the third point of proposition 4.2

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Notice that $X$ is an open set but also a closed set at the same time, so do $\emptyset$. In this such case, we call the set a **clopen** set.

- In every topological space, $(X,\tau)$, both $X$ and $\emptyset$ are clopen.

- In a discrete space, all subsets of $X$ are clopen.

- In an indiscrete space, the only clopen subsets are $X$ and $\emptyset$.
:::

## Closed Set - Standard Topology

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Any closed interval in standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is a closed set.
:::

Take a closed interval, $[a,b]$, then the complement of it is $\mathbb{R} \setminus [a,b] =(-∞,a) \cup(b,∞)$, which is an open set.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Each singleton set, $\{a\}$, in standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$ is a closed set.
:::

Take any singleton set, $\{a\}$, then the complement of it is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{a\} =(-∞,a) \cup(a,∞)$, which is an open set.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
A half-open interval, such as $[a,b)$, is neither open nor closed in standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$.
:::

Take a half-open interval, $[a,b)$, then the complement of it is $\mathbb{R} \setminus [a,b) =(-∞,a) \cup[b,∞)$, which is a union of an open set and another half-open interval, so its not an open set.

## Recap - Interior and Closure

\vspace{2mm}

::: block
### Definition 4.3

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X,\tau)$. The closure of $A$ is the **intersection** of all closed sets containing $A$:

$$Cl(A) = \overline{A} = \bigcap \{F \mid F \text{ is a closed set and } A \subseteq F\}$$
:::

::: block
### Definition 3.4

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X,\tau)$. The **interior** of $A$, denoted by $Int(A)$ or $\mathring{A}$, is the union of all open sets contained in $A$:

$$Int(A) = \mathring{A} = \bigcup \{U \in \tau \mid U \subseteq A\}$$
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Consider $A=[0,1)$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology. Then $Cl(A)=[0,1]$ and $Int(A)=(0,1)$.
:::

## Boundary

\vspace{2mm}

::: block
### Definition 4.4

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X,\tau)$. The **boundary** of $A$, denoted $\partial A$, is the set:

$$\partial A=Cl(A)-Int(A)=Cl(A)\setminus Int(A)$$
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
Consider $A=[0,1)$ as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology. Then $Cl(A)=[0,1]$ and $Int(A)=(0,1)$.

$\partial A=[0,1]-(0,1)=[0,1]\setminus(0,1)=\{0,1\}$
:::

## Boundary (cont.)

\vspace{2mm}

This theorem gives conditions that help us to determine whether or not a point $x$ lies in the boundary of a set $A$.

::: block
### Theorem 4.5

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X,\tau)$ and let $x$ be a point in $X$. Then $x\in \partial A$ if and only if every neighborhood of $x$ intersects both $A$ and $X\setminus A$, or

$$x \in \partial A \iff  \forall U \in \tau \text{ with } x \in U, \; (U \cap A \neq \emptyset) \land (U \setminus A \neq \emptyset) $$
:::

noted that $U\cap(X\setminus A)$ can be simplify to $U\setminus A$ as illustrated below,

## Relation

::: block
### Theorem 4.6

Let $A$ be a subset of a topological space $(X,\tau)$,

\(i\) $\partial A =\partial A^c$.

\(ii\) $Cl(A)=A\cup \partial A$ and $Cl(A^c)=A^c \cup \partial A$.

\(iii\) $Cl(A)\cap Cl(A^c)=\partial A$.

\(iv\) $Cl(A^c)^c=A\setminus \partial A=Int(A)$.
:::

![](week5/image4.png){fig-align="center" width="72%"}

## Relation (cont.)

Let $(X,\tau)$ be a topological space and $A$ and $B$ be subsets of $X$.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(i\) If $U$ is an open set in $X$ and $U\subset A$, then $U\subset Int(A)$.
:::

Since we define Interior as a union of all open set, so $U$ must be one of them.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(ii\) If $C$ is a closed set in $X$ and $A\subset C$, then $Cl(A) \subset C$.
:::

Since we define closure as intersection of all closed set, so the closure itself must be a subset of any $C$.

![](week5/image3.png){fig-align="center" width="51%"}

## Relation (cont.)

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(iii\) If $A\subseteq B$ then $Int(A) \subseteq Int(B)$. \vspace{2mm}

\(iv\) If $A\subseteq B$ then $Cl(A) \subseteq Cl(B)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(v\) $A$ is open if and only if $A=Int(A)$.
:::

For example, let $A=(a,b)$, then $Int(A)=(a,b)$. So we can see that now $A=Int(A)$. we know that an open interval is an open set.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(vi\) $A$ is closed if and only if $A=Cl(A)$. Noted that $\partial A \subseteq A$.
:::

For example, let $A=[a,b]$, then $Cl(A)=[a,b]$. So we can see that now $A=Cl(A)$. we know that a closed interval is a closed set.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(vii\) $Cl(A)=Int(A)∪∂A$.
:::

## Relation (cont.)

![](week5/image4.png){fig-align="center" width="54%"}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(viii\) $Int(A^c)=Cl(A)^c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(ix\) $Cl(A^c)=Int(A)^c$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(x\) $Int(A)\cup Int(B) \subset Int(A \cup B)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(xi\) $Int(A) \cap Int(B) = Int(A \cap B)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
\(xii\) $Int(A) \subseteq A \subseteq Cl(A)$ and $\partial A \subseteq Cl(A)$
:::
